entities.name: Nasir-ol-Molk Mosque
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Nasir ol-Molk Mosque (Pink Mosque) in Shiraz, Iran, completed in 1888 under the Qajar dynasty, is one of the most visually spectacular mosques in the world — its southern iwan (prayer hall) is filled with floor-to-ceiling colored stained glass that, when morning sunlight enters, floods the interior with a kaleidoscopic spectrum of pink, purple, orange, and blue light across the Persian carpets, creating what photographers call 'a living painting.' The mosque's unusual pink tile exterior and stained glass integration make it unique in Persian mosque architecture.

Mirza Hasan Ali Nasir ol-Molk, a regent-level Qajar official, commissioned the mosque from architects Mohammad Hassan Memar and Mohammad Reza Kashi-Paz. Construction took 12 years (1876-1888). The stained glass — Iranian craftsmen working in a tradition more common in European Gothic cathedrals — was integrated into the arched windows of the prayer hall at a scale and with a color palette unprecedented in Iranian mosque architecture. The morning light effect (best experienced 7:30-10:00 AM, October through March) is fleeting but extraordinary.

The mosque's muqarnas (honeycomb stalactite ceiling vaults) in the eastern iwan represent one of Iran's finest examples — geometric complexity creating three-dimensional shadow patterns. The geometric tile work (girih tiles) in the courtyard and the painted plaster arabesques combine to make Nasir ol-Molk among the most ornamentally complex mosques in Persia. The mosque's Instagram fame (discovered by travel photographers around 2015) transformed it into Iran's most photographed building, raising complex questions about religious sites and tourism.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Nasir ol-Molk Mosque's morning stained-glass light effect — a Qajar innovation borrowed from Gothic cathedral tradition and applied to Persian mosque architecture — created the most visually spectacular interior in Iranian religious architecture, demonstrating that borrowing across traditions can generate unprecedented beauty.
